All three solutions look wrong. I did not verify the true minimum rigorously, and my belief that it is ⌊n/2⌋·C(q,2) rests on a heuristic perturbation argument and what I recall of the known result.

**Solution 1.** Its star construction is not bowtie-free. Take the star centre u ∈ X, two leaves v₁ and v₂, and two distinct vertices y, y′ ∈ Y. The triangles u v₁ y and u v₂ y′ share only u, so they form a bowtie. The claim of zero bowties is false, and the answer 0 is wrong.

**Solution 2.** It splits the q added edges evenly between the two parts. The justification is a first-order perturbation estimate, which is not enough here. At first order the shifts are equal, but at second order the antisymmetric eigenvector couples to the perturbation only when the edges are unbalanced between the parts. This gives the unbalanced graph a slightly larger spectral radius than the split graph. So the split graph likely has λ below λ(K^q), which violates the constraint, and the claimed value nq²/8 is unsupported. It is also only an asymptotic approximation. The expected answer is most likely ⌊n/2⌋·C(q,2).

**Solution 3.** It uses the same unjustified splitting argument. In its final check it treats equal first-order shifts as equal spectral radii, which ignores the second-order effect above. Its exact formula is therefore also unsupported.

VERDICT 1: REJECT
VERDICT 2: REJECT
VERDICT 3: REJECT
